Tiglath-pileser III
TIG-lath-py-LEE-zer thuh thurd
proper noun
Assyrian royal name; the king of Assyria (also called Pul in Scripture) who carried away the tribes beyond Jordan and Galilee.

Biblical Definition

Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, called Pul in the Scriptures, was the powerful Assyrian monarch whom the LORD used as His rod against a faithless Israel. When Menahem king of Israel gave Pul a thousand talents of silver that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom, the tribute only delayed judgment. Later, when Pekah reigned, Tiglath-pileser came and took Ijon, and Abel-beth-maachah, and the cities of Naphtali, and carried the people captive to Assyria—the first great deportation of the northern tribes. And when Ahaz king of Judah, threatened by Syria and Israel, hired Tiglath-pileser with the treasures of the temple to deliver him, the Assyrian came, but distressed him and strengthened him not, for Ahaz had trusted the arm of Assyria rather than the LORD. The Chronicler records that God stirred up the spirit of Tiglath-pileser to carry away the transjordan tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh, because they had transgressed against the God of their fathers and gone a whoring after the gods of the peoples whom God destroyed before them. The dictionary honors the record of Tiglath-pileser as a testimony that the LORD wields even pagan empires as His instruments of chastisement upon His covenant people, and that to trust the arm of flesh against the LORD is to be distressed by the very power one hired.

Webster 1828 Definition

King of Assyria (called Pul); the LORD’s rod against faithless Israel, who deported the northern and transjordan tribes and distressed Ahaz who hired him.

TIGLATH-PILESER III, king of Assyria, called Pul in Scripture.

Menahem of Israel paid him a thousand talents of silver as tribute.

He carried Naphtali and the transjordan tribes captive to Assyria.

Ahaz of Judah hired him, but he distressed and strengthened not.

The LORD’s rod against a faithless and idolatrous people.

Key Scripture

2Ki 15:29 — "In the days of Pekah king of Israel came Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor, and Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria."

1Ch 5:26 — "And the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away, even the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and brought them unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day."

2Ch 28:20 — "And Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria came unto him, and distressed him, but strengthened him not."

Isa 10:5 — "O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation."

Modern Corruption

Tiglath-pileser is read as mere imperial conqueror in a political history; Scripture names him the LORD’s rod of chastisement upon a faithless people.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the merely political-historical reading that treats Tiglath-pileser as one more ambitious conqueror in the rise of Assyrian power, subordinating the Chronicler’s theological judgment to the metrics of empire. Scripture sees deeper: the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul to carry away the transjordan tribes because they had transgressed against the God of their fathers (1 Chr 5:26). The conqueror’s ambition was the unwitting instrument of the LORD’s chastisement.

The principle to recover is the LORD’s sovereign use of pagan empires as the rod of His anger. He calls Assyria the rod of mine anger, the staff in their hand is mine indignation (Isa 10:5)—a nation that knew Him not, yet served His purpose against a faithless covenant people. The account also warns against trusting the arm of flesh: Ahaz hired Tiglath-pileser against his enemies, but the Assyrian came and distressed him and strengthened him not (2 Chr 28:20), for he had leaned on Assyria rather than the LORD. To use the world against the world, forsaking God, is to be wounded by the very power one trusted.

Hebrew Roots

Assyrian king, called Pul; the LORD’s rod against faithless Israel, who deported the northern and transjordan tribes and distressed the unbelieving Ahaz.

Tiglath-pileser III — king of Assyria, called Pul in Scripture.

Took tribute from Menahem; carried Naphtali captive (2Ki 15:29).

Deported Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh for their sin (1Ch 5:26).

Distressed Ahaz, who hired him against his enemies (2Ch 28:20).

The rod of the LORD’s anger against an idolatrous people (Isa 10:5).

Usage

"Tiglath-pileser carried the transjordan tribes captive for their idolatry."

"Ahaz hired the Assyrian, but he distressed him and strengthened not."

"The LORD calls Assyria the rod of His anger against His faithless people."
